:::{#def-vector-p-norm}
#### Vector $p$-norm ($\ell_p$ norm, $\ell_1$ norm, $\ell_2$ norm, infinity norm)

For a vector $\vx = (x_1, \ldots, x_p) \in \reals^p$ and any real number $k \ge 1$,
the **vector $p$-norm** (or **$\ell_p$ norm**, traditionally named with parameter $p$ but denoted here with exponent $k$ to avoid clashing with the ambient vector dimension $p$) is:

$$
\norm{\vx}_k \eqdef \paren{\sumip \abs{x_i}^k}^{1/k}.
$$

The cases $k = 1$ and $k = 2$ are named the **$\ell_1$ norm** (also the **taxicab norm** or **Manhattan norm**)
and the **$\ell_2$ norm**.
The **infinity norm** (also the **$\ell_\infty$ norm**, **maximum norm**, or **Chebyshev norm**) is defined separately by

$$
\norm{\vx}_\infty \eqdef \max_{1 \le i \le p} \abs{x_i}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-vector-p-norm}
#### Calculating $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$ norms

For $\vx = (3, -4) \in \reals^2$:

- $\ell_1$ norm:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \norm{\vx}_1 &= \abs{3} + \abs{-4} \\
  &= 3 + 4 \\
  &= 7.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- $\ell_2$ norm:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \norm{\vx}_2 &= \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} \\
  &= \sqrt{9 + 16} \\
  &= \sqrt{25} \\
  &= 5.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- $\ell_\infty$ norm:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \norm{\vx}_\infty &= \max(\abs{3}, \abs{-4}) \\
  &= 4.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

Notice that $4 \le 5 \le 7$. For any vector $\vx \in \reals^p$, the norms satisfy the chain of inequalities:

$$
\norm{\vx}_\infty \le \norm{\vx}_2 \le \norm{\vx}_1 \le \sqrt{p}\,\norm{\vx}_2 \le p\,\norm{\vx}_\infty.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-vector-norms-sparsity}
#### Unit balls and regularization in machine learning

The unit ball in $\reals^2$ under the $\ell_p$ norm is the set $\cb{\vx \in \reals^2 : \norm{\vx}_k \le 1}$:

- For $k = 1$, the unit ball is a diamond (cross-polytope) with sharp vertices along the coordinate axes $(\pm 1, 0)$ and $(0, \pm 1)$.
- For $k = 2$, the unit ball is the smooth round Euclidean unit disk.
- For $k = \infty$, the unit ball is an axis-aligned square with vertices $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$.

In regression and machine learning, adding an $\ell_1$ penalty (Lasso regularization) to an objective function encourages sparse solutions:
the level curves of the loss function tend to make contact with the sharp corners of the $\ell_1$ unit ball on the coordinate axes, setting irrelevant feature weights exactly to zero.
In contrast, the smooth spherical $\ell_2$ penalty (Ridge regularization) shrinks all weights toward zero without setting them exactly to zero.

:::
